summary: Specifies a TLS extension for negotiating the Token Binding protocol version and key parameters. Negotiation in TLS 1.3 and later is out of scope.

eli5.summary: Before using fingerprint tickets, the two sides agree on which kind and which version.

questions: what is the token_binding tls extension
does token binding work with tls 1.3
subtitle: The TLS extension that lets a client and server agree on Token Binding version and key type during the handshake.

tldr.problem: Before Token Binding can be used, the client and server must agree on the protocol version and the signature algorithm and length of the binding key, ideally without extra network round trips.
tldr.mechanism: A new TLS extension called token_binding carries the client's highest version and a preference-ordered list of key parameters in the ClientHello, and the server answers in the ServerHello with the lower version and exactly one chosen key parameter.
tldr.outcome: The choice is protected by the TLS handshake itself. With TLS 1.2 and older, Token Binding is only negotiated if extended master secret and renegotiation indication are also negotiated, and TLS 1.3 is out of scope.

today: RFC 8472 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It covers TLS 1.2 and earlier only and leaves TLS 1.3 to a separate document.

sections.title: Why Negotiation Is Needed
sections.content:
To use the Token Binding protocol of RFC 8471, the client and server must agree on the protocol version and the parameters of the Token Binding key: the signature algorithm and its length. This document defines a TLS extension that does this without adding network round trips in TLS 1.2 and earlier.

Negotiation with TLS 1.3 and later is out of scope. The RFC points to a separate document for TLS 1.3 and notes that the TLS 1.2 specification it cites (RFC 5246) has been obsoleted by RFC 8446.
sections.eli5: Before you swap fingerprint tickets, you and the shop have to agree on which kind of fingerprint and which rule book to use. This note says how to agree during the greeting.

sections.title: The ClientHello Extension
sections.content:
The client sends a token_binding extension, extension type 24, in its ClientHello. Its data is a TokenBindingParameters value holding a token_binding_version (a major and a minor octet) and a key_parameters_list of 1 to 255 identifiers in descending order of preference. The identifiers are those from the registry created by RFC 8471: rsa2048_pkcs1.5 (0), rsa2048_pss (1) and ecdsap256 (2).

If the client supports several versions it SHOULD offer its latest. If it supports {1, 0} and {0, 13}, it SHOULD indicate {1, 0}. The server MAY pick any lower version. If the client does not support the version the server picks, the connection simply proceeds without Token Binding. The two-octet version form is only for human convenience and has no protocol significance.
sections.eli5: The visitor says the newest rule book they know and lists the kinds of fingerprints they can do, best first.

sections.title: The Server's Answer
sections.content:
A server that supports Token Binding includes the token_binding extension in its ServerHello only if all of these hold:

  • It supports the offered version or a lower one.
  • It finds acceptable key parameters in the client's list. It ignores identifiers it does not recognize.
  • With TLS 1.2 or older, it is also negotiating the extended master secret (RFC 7627) and renegotiation indication (RFC 5746) extensions.

The reply has the same structure. Its version is the lower of the client's offered version and the server's highest supported version. Its list holds exactly one identifier. The server MUST only choose an identifier the client offered and SHOULD choose its most preferred one that the client also advertised. If it supports none, it MUST NOT include the extension.
sections.eli5: The shop picks the older of the two rule books and one kind of fingerprint from the visitor's list, preferably its own favorite. If none match, it says nothing and they skip fingerprints.

sections.title: Client Checks and Resumption
sections.content:
The client MUST end the handshake with a fatal unsupported_extension alert if the server's extension is wrong in any of these ways:

  • The client never sent the extension.
  • The version is higher than the client advertised.
  • The list has more than one identifier.
  • The list has an identifier the client did not advertise.
  • TLS 1.2 or older is used but extended master secret and renegotiation indication were not negotiated.

Otherwise the version and key parameters are definitive for the connection, and the client MUST use the negotiated key parameters in the provided_token_binding of RFC 8471. Renegotiation can renegotiate them on the same connection.

Negotiation happens per TLS connection, so both sides include the extension in full handshakes and in abbreviated handshakes that resume a session. If negotiation fails, applications may carry on as usual, shorten token lifetimes, require stronger authentication or end the connection.
sections.eli5: The visitor double-checks the shop's answer. If the shop picks something that was not offered, the visitor hangs up on the spot.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
Downgrade attacks are covered by TLS itself: it detects handshake modification by active attackers, so an attacker cannot remove or change the extension without breaking the handshake. The signature algorithm and key length of a provided_token_binding MUST match what was negotiated.

Token Binding relies on TLS exporters (RFC 5705), and the triple handshake attack on TLS 1.2 and older lets an attacker synchronize keying material between connections and replay bound tokens. So Token Binding MUST NOT be negotiated with those versions unless extended master secret and renegotiation indication are also negotiated.

IANA registers token_binding with value 24 in the "TLS ExtensionType Values" registry, marked Recommended: Yes. No new registrations are made in the Token Binding Key Parameters registry.
sections.eli5: Because the greeting is protected, nobody in the middle can sneak in and change the deal. Old versions of the greeting have a known trick, so extra safety steps are required with them.
